content:
1. Verify the exact symptom and scope of the failure. Open a terminal on the client machine or jump host that is experiencing the issue. Run curl -v http://localhost:8080/api/health to confirm the response code is 502 Bad Gateway. If the request times out instead, the problem may be a network partition or a hung process rather than an upstream failure. Check the headers returned by the proxy. Look specifically for Server: nginx/1.24.0 or similar identifiers. This tells you which layer is generating the error. If the header says Apache, the diagnosis path changes entirely. Focus on the specific endpoint that is failing. Test multiple endpoints to see if the 502 is global or isolated to a specific route. Run curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8080/api/users and compare it with curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8080/static/image.png. If static assets load but API calls fail, the backend application server is likely down or overloaded.

2. Inspect the reverse proxy error logs immediately. For Nginx, the primary error log is usually located at /var/log/nginx/error.log. Execute tail -n 100 /var/log/nginx/error.log to see recent entries. Look for lines containing upstream timed out, connect() failed, or no live upstreams. If you see connect() failed (111: Connection refused), the backend service is not listening on the expected port. If you see upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out), the backend is running but too slow to respond within the proxy timeout window. For Apache httpd, check /var/log/apache2/error.log or /var/log/httpd/error_log. Use grep -i "bad gateway" /var/log/apache2/error.log | tail -20 to find relevant entries. The logs will often include the IP address and port of the upstream server that failed. Note this address for the next step. If the logs are rotated, check older files like error.log.1 or use zcat /var/log/nginx/error.log.1.gz | grep "502" to search through compressed archives.

3. Verify that the backend service is actually running and listening on the correct port. Identify the upstream address defined in your proxy configuration. For Nginx, this is typically found in the upstream block or the proxy_pass directive. Open /etc/nginx/sites-available/default or /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf. Look for lines like proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;. The port number here is critical. On the server hosting the backend, run ss -tlnp | grep :3000 to check if a process is listening on that port. If no output appears, the backend service is not running or is bound to a different interface. If you see LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:3000 0.0.0.0:* users:(("node",pid=1234,fd=20)), the service is active. If it is bound to 0.0.0.0, it is accessible from any interface. If it is bound to a specific IP that does not match the proxy target, there is a configuration mismatch.

4. Check the system status of the backend process using systemd or your init system. Run systemctl status nodejs-app.service to see if the service is active and running. Look for the Active: line. It should say active (running). If it says failed or inactive (dead), the service has crashed or was stopped. Examine the most recent logs for the service with journalctl -u nodejs-app.service -n 50 --no-pager. This will show you if the application threw an exception during startup or if it ran out of memory. If the service is restarting frequently, check the status output for a counter like "Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL". Status 9 indicates the OOM killer terminated the process. Run dmesg | tail -50 to confirm if the kernel logged an Out of memory: Kill process event. If so, your application is consuming too much RAM and needs optimization or more resources.

5. Test connectivity between the proxy and the backend directly. From the machine running the reverse proxy, run telnet 127.0.0.1 3000 to test raw TCP connectivity. If you get a "Connection refused" error, the port is closed. If you get a blank screen or a connection established message, the TCP handshake is successful. You can also use nc -zv 127.0.0.1 3000 for a faster check. If the proxy and backend are on different machines, replace 127.0.0.1 with the backend IP address. Run ping <backend_ip> to verify basic network reachability. If ping fails, check firewall rules. On Linux, use iptables -L -n | grep DROP to see if any rules are blocking traffic. Check for cloud security groups if you are in AWS, Azure, or GCP. Ensure that the inbound rule allows traffic from the proxy IP on the backend port.

6. Analyze the application logs for unhandled exceptions or errors. Locate the log file for your backend application. Common locations include /var/log/myapp/app.log, /home/user/project/logs/error.log, or stdout captured by systemd. Run tail -f /var/log/myapp/app.log to watch live output while triggering a request from the client. Observe if any error stack traces appear when the 502 occurs. Look for messages like "ECONNRESET", "Socket hang up", or "Unhandled promise rejection". If you are using a Node.js application, check for memory leaks or infinite loops that might be causing the process to become unresponsive. For Python applications, look for traceback errors in the log file. Use grep -i "error" /var/log/myapp/app.log | tail -20 to filter for relevant lines. If the logs are empty, ensure that logging is configured correctly and that log files have sufficient disk space.

7. Check resource utilization on the backend server. High CPU or memory usage can cause timeouts. Run top -c to see real-time CPU usage per process. Identify if your application process is consuming 100% of one or more CPU cores. If so, there may be a performance bottleneck in the code. Run free -h to check available memory and swap usage. If available memory is near zero and swap is heavily used, the system is under memory pressure. This can cause slow response times that trigger proxy timeouts. Use iostat -x 1 5 to monitor disk I/O statistics. Look for high %util values on your storage devices. If disk I/O is saturated, database queries or file operations may be too slow, leading to 502 errors. Consider adding more RAM or optimizing database indexes if I/O wait is high.

8. Review the proxy timeout settings in your configuration file. Open your Nginx configuration file again. Look for proxy_read_timeout, proxy_connect_timeout, and proxy_send_timeout directives. The default values are often 60 seconds. If your backend takes longer than this to respond, Nginx will return a 502. Test with a simple curl command that forces a delay: curl -v --max-time 90 http://localhost:8080/slow-endpoint. If the request succeeds after 70 seconds but fails at 60 seconds, you need to increase the timeout values. Add or modify proxy_read_timeout 120s; in your location block. After making changes, validate the configuration with nginx -t. If the syntax is correct, reload Nginx with systemctl reload nginx. Do not restart the service if possible, as reloading preserves existing connections.

9. Check for SSL/TLS certificate issues if using HTTPS. Even though 502 is a gateway error, upstream SSL mismatches can cause failures. Ensure that the backend server presents a valid certificate if the proxy expects one. Run openssl s_client -connect backend_ip:443 -servername example.com to test the TLS handshake. Look for "Verify return code" in the output. If it is not 0 (ok), there may be a certificate chain issue or hostname mismatch. In your Nginx config, if you are using proxy_pass https://..., ensure that proxy_ssl_verify off; is set during testing if you have self-signed certificates, though this is not recommended for production. Check if the backend application is correctly terminating SSL or if it expects plain HTTP from the proxy. A mismatch here will cause connection resets that manifest as 502 errors.

10. Investigate load balancer health checks if applicable. If your architecture includes a load balancer in front of the backend, ensure that the backend nodes are marked as healthy. Log into your cloud provider console or run kubectl get pods if using Kubernetes. In Kubernetes, check pod status with kubectl get pods -n production. Look for CrashLoopBackOff or Error states. If a pod is restarting, it will not pass health checks, and the load balancer will route traffic to other nodes. If all nodes are unhealthy, you may get 502 errors. Run kubectl describe pod <pod_name> to see events related to liveness probes failing. Check the logs of the specific pod with kubectl logs -f <pod_name>. Ensure that your liveness probe endpoint is responding quickly and correctly.

11. Examine network interface statistics for dropped packets or errors. Run ifconfig eth0 or ip -s link show eth0 to see packet counters.
